nameStory: Korean bushclover gets its name from Korea, one of the countries where it naturally grows in East Asia. Despite being called 'bushclover,' it's not actually a true clover but belongs to a different group within the legume family. The 'bush' part of the name refers to its bushy, spreading growth habit that can form small mounds.
description: Korean bushclover is a low-growing annual herb that spreads along the ground or grows upright to about 2 feet tall. It has the classic three-leaflet leaves typical of legumes, with small purple-blue flowers tucked along the stems. This Asian native was brought to America in 1919 and has since naturalized across the eastern United States. It forms bushy patches that provide food for wildlife and livestock.

idTips.label: Stipules
idTips.description: Look for large, papery, wing-like structures at the base of each leaf stem - these stipules are especially noticeable on young leaves and feel thin and dry to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three oval leaflets per leaf, each about the size of your thumbnail, with a smooth texture and subtle veining

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny purple-blue flowers appear in clusters of 1-5 tucked into the leaf joints, though some flowers never open and self-pollinate in secret

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading mats or grows upright to knee-high, with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat wiry but flexible

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, flattened pods that contain a single seed and make a soft rattling sound when dry and shaken

habitat: Korean bushclover thrives in disturbed soils, roadsides, old fields, and areas where the ground has been cleared or compacted. It prefers full sun to partial shade and tolerates poor, dry soils where other plants struggle. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species in abandoned lots, field edges, and recovering disturbed sites.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small three-leaflet seedlings, with the distinctive papery stipules most visible on young plants.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and begin flowering, producing both the visible purple-blue flowers and hidden self-pollinating ones.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn brown, while the entire plant begins to die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Plants have died completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: Korean bushclover produces two completely different types of flowers on the same plant - some that open normally to receive pollen from bees, and secret 'stealth' flowers that never open and fertilize themselves, ensuring the plant can reproduce even when pollinators are scarce!
confusionNotes: The large, papery stipules at the leaf bases are your best clue to separate Korean bushclover from its close relative Japanese clover, which has much smaller, less noticeable stipules. Remember: Korean = conspicuous papery wings at the leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a clover, Korean bushclover isn't a true clover (Trifolium) but belongs to a different genus entirely. The USDA intentionally introduced this plant nearly a century ago to help restore damaged mining sites and prevent soil erosion, showing how sometimes 'weedy' plants can be environmental helpers.
compareHints: Korean bushclover is easily distinguished from its only New England relative, Japanese clover, by those prominent papery stipules at the leaf bases - Japanese clover has tiny, barely visible stipules. Both species often grow together, so you can directly compare the leaf bases to see the dramatic difference in stipule size.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Japanese clover is very similar to its relative Korean bushclover, but Korean bushclover tends to grow more upright rather than spreading along the ground.
